deep.reconstruction:
The page is a table of quadratic residues, continuing the previous page (421–439) and the next (467–487). There are no derivations; each entry is a prime p followed by a list of quadratic residues a, i.e. a with (a/p) = +1.

Marginal signs:
- The small mark above each prime (− over 443 and 463; + over 449, 457 and 461; the same pattern on the neighbouring pages) records the residue character of −1. That is, (−1/p) = (−1)^((p−1)/2): '+' when p ≡ 1 (mod 4) and '−' when p ≡ 3 (mod 4).
- For p ≡ 3 (mod 4) (443, 463) the list is prefixed '+' and runs over the whole range 1..p−1. These lists hold 221 and 231 entries, which equals (p−1)/2, as it must. Since −1 is a non-residue, a is a residue exactly when p−a is not.
- For p ≡ 1 (mod 4) (449, 457, 461) the list is prefixed '∓' (meaning ±a). It runs only over 1..(p−1)/2, because a and −a then have the same character. The counts are 112, 114 and 115, i.e. (p−1)/4 rounded.

Method (inferred by me): probably sieving, using multiplicativity of the Legendre symbol from the characters of small primes, or by squaring and reducing. The corrections show checking. For 443 he inserted 52, 165, 271, 435 and 437 and struck 73, 99, 426 and the non-residue(s) between 301 and 307. For 449 he inserted 50 and 59 and struck a non-residue at 52 and another at 201. For 457 he inserted 56, 119 and 127 and struck 166 or 167. For 463 he inserted 185 and struck 186 or 187. I checked every insertion and deletion I could identify against the Legendre symbol; all are correct.

results.usually_credited_to: Residue tables go back to Euler, Legendre and Gauss. Gauss's Disquisitiones (1801), Table II, gives the characters of small primes for p<1000.

results.what: Use of (−1/p)=(−1)^((p−1)/2) to halve the table for p≡1 mod 4, listing ±a up to (p−1)/2.

deep.surprise_reason: Routine computational residue tables of the kind Gauss is well known to have compiled (cf. Disquisitiones Art. 99 and its tables); no new mathematics.
